#8379. How to Navigate the Tariff Circus

Quite accidentally, it looks like we timed our last talk about the stock market pretty darned well. Back in February 2025, the market put the perfect cap on a multi year climb before stepping onto the wild roller coaster we’re currently riding. Since then it has seen some of the steepest drops and recoveries in history, losing a full 20% of its value at the bottom while somehow managing to end up right back near the peak as I’m writing this.

And although stock market volatility doesn’t always come with an easily labeled explanation, this time the reason seems pretty clear: it’s the Tariffs.

As our financial world has been whipped around like a circus tent in a hurricane for the last several months, almost everyone who has a stake in this country has been wondering what to make of it.

As I write this, we still don’t know the outcome of the worldwide tariff and trade battle that our unpredictable government has unleashed upon the world. But we’re already seeing the results: businesses are bracing for massive changes, currencies and interest rates are reacting, and regular investors like you and me are wondering what the future holds for our early retirement funds. Surveying my own group of friends, the reactions span the whole range of emotions from “this is a giant Nothingburger” to “we’re all totally screwed.”

So what’s the real answer? To get closer to that, we should start with the most basic question of:

A tariff is just a sales tax charged by our government on goods which are imported into the country.  They are paid by whoever is doing the importing – meaning you if you order something like an e-bike directly from a company in China, or by companies like Amazon, Walmart, or Apple which import products from other countries by the shipload.

But in the end, the tariffs aren’t paid by China or Amazon or Apple. They are paid by you, the end consumer, because if their cost of goods increases, a retailer is of course going to raise their prices to continue to make a profit.

Tariffs also affect companies directly: if Home Depot wants to build a new store or Chevron needs a new oil rig, the tariffs on imported steel, copper, lumber and a million other components will raise the cost of these construction projects. And they raise the cost of housing, because most of the building materials in houses come from multiple countries as well.

On average, tariffs will result in higher prices for everything just like any other broad-based sales tax. And just like most other taxes, the overall effect is to slow the economy and reduce our spending power. On the positive side, all that tax money flows into the government’s pocket which could help fund the national budget and even reduce the deficit.

Of course, every government needs at least some tax revenue to function, so it makes sense to use some mix of sales, income and corporate taxes to get there. The most important part is that the levels need to be as low as possible while still keeping the country running well, and as fair and predictable as possible, so that people and businesses have an incentive to work hard and the ability to plan far into the future.

And that’s where our current tariff regime gets it completely backwards. Donald Trump is throwing around random, extremely high tariff numbers as threats, then walking them back and changing them on an almost daily basis..

Whoa, that Sounds Mostly Bad – Is There a Good Side of Tariffs?

Sometimes, a country will use tariffs to protect their own domestic industries. For example, if you put a tax on imported Hondas, then General Motors cars will gain a competitive advantage – so GM will make more money. In this example, most consumers end up losing due to increased prices and decreased selection. But at least domestic auto manufacturers and their employees are happy.

This can be strategic (for example we might want to slap a tax on imported fighter jets to make sure Boeing and Lockheed can remain in business, for national defense purposes.) Or it can be corrupt (a politician might receive funding from kingpins in the steel industry, and in return then push through tariffs on imported steel to protect the profits of US steelmakers.)

And this isn’t just a Trump or Republican thing either – Joe Biden used tariffs during his terms in an attempt to please swing-state voters. One of the worst examples was a tax on imported solar panel components (which Trump has since raised even further, proving that Boneheadedness can be Bipartisan). These are sheets of cheap glass that literally pump the cheapest energy and easiest wealth into your country for 30 years as soon as you plug them in. Cheap energy lowers everyone’s cost of living while also boosting industry. There is no good reason to block such wealth from flowing across your borders.

Let’s go back to that hypothetical tax on Hondas, and let’s say it’s a big one like $5000. At that level, many buyers will start heading over to the GM dealer next door to consider what he’s selling. Sure, the GM cars may not be as good, but for five grand some people are going to settle in order to save some money.

Because of this, GM’s sales go up. So they hire more employees and build more factories. They might even develop some new models and new technologies in response to all that new demand. More people learn advanced skills and in the best case it becomes a virtuous circle.

But in exchange for this boom in the auto industry, everyone else has to pay more for slightly shittier cars and trucks. Higher vehicle prices means Amazon will have to spend more on their delivery fleet, so they will raise prices slightly on everything they sell. Somewhere a startup company or a medical breakthrough will be just a bit less likely to happen, because they are operating in an environment that is just a bit more expensive and a bit less efficient.

On top of that, with GM liberated from the hassle of competing with Honda, it will have less incentive to innovate and streamline itself. So its overall trajectory will be slower and less efficient even if its profits are higher.

This big picture effect is why most economists agree that tariffs should be used very sparingly. They almost always cause unexpected damage, decrease overall employment and slow down an economy, but sometimes (like for food security or national defense) those costs are worth paying.

So Why is Donald Trump Throwing Around Tariffs Like They Are The Best Thing Ever?

This has been confusing to almost everyone. If you take him at his word, he appears to have a Bizarro Opposite Universe belief system about economics. Donald has claimed in speeches that the tariffs will somehow make us wealthier. He’s focusing on the first-order effects like GM hiring more workers, while completely ignoring the fact that everything else in the country gets less efficient in exchange.

But when he announces larger tariffs, share prices go down, because everyone who actually runs or invests in US companies knows that of course they will make less money on average. When tariffs are paused or reduced, share prices go back up. Yet he keeps wielding the threats and we go back and forth.

It seems to be obvious to everyone except Donald himself that Tariffs are just a national sales tax rather than some clever sneaky strategic weapon, which leads to various theories that okay, maybe he knows that too but is just pretending in order to gain some influence.

So right now our entire economy is subject to the whims of a single person.. And as long as this is the case, we’re just the same as any other dictatorship – something our constitution was supposed to prevent with the whole “three independent branches of government” thing.

But presidents have tried to break out of their constitutional cage and get more power many times in the past, and this is just the latest example. The real test will be if our system eventually manages to stop this abuse and put itself back in balance as it always has in the past. You can already see this fight beginning to play out in our court system, in this Economist article:

Even without the 145% nonsense numbers that were thrown around a few months ago, they are still far higher than they have been in the last 75 years or more. While it would be hard to pin down the current numbers in a stationary blog post like this one, the key thing to remember is that our current US economy is built around very low tariffs and relatively free trade.

Why haven’t I noticed Prices Going Up Yet?

While the US economy is fueled by a constant stream of cargo ships, as a whole we function like the biggest cargo ship of all: we have a huge inventory and it takes a while to change directions.

So in normal times, we already have several months of inventory of most things in the country. And then when all this drama started, importers started placing even more orders to stockpile things in advance before the tariffs hit. And now that they are in place, we’re importing a lot less stuff.

For now, we’re still using up the stockpiled inventory, but imports have dropped significantly so we’re quickly running out of cheap goods. If that happens, we will probably start seeing shortages and price increases throughout this summer or fall. For some things like plastic party trinkets, we can do just fine without. But if we lose access to core useful things like tools and machinery, the economic consequences will be much less fun.

The most important phrase to remember in US politics and economics is the phrase “This too shall pass.” The only mystery right now is that we don’t know exactly how it will pass. So we could sketch out a few scenarios:

1) The current crazy-high tariffs really do stick around:

I personally think this is the less likely scenario because nobody really wants it. But just as a thought experiment, it might go something like this:

2) They do end up being just a negotiating tactic and we go back to mostly low tariffs.

In other words, the best way to win the tariff game is not to play it.

Just as much of US prosperity is built upon our huge population of 330 million people living in 50 states with open borders and no trade restrictions, all (friendly) countries of the world can benefit from the free exchange of goods, services and even people. We’re all human beings and if we treat each other with a collaborative respect, we all grow richer.

I started writing this article on April 2nd, when Donald announced his “Liberation Day” and the stock market reacted with the biggest drop since 1932. Some people panicked and locked in big losses despite decades of warnings from your favorite financial bloggers, like this unfortunate soul in the comments to a JL Collins post:

But as I watched over the next two months, we have bounced our way back up – with each drop in proposed tariffs triggering a corresponding increase in stock prices (a measure of investor enthusiasm of how bright our future looks).

Right now, the US stock market is just about back to its all-time high. This doesn’t match with our current level of tariffs, which are still about seven times higher than they were before the circus opened. But it shows that investors believe it’s all going to end with a truce and a resumption of free-ish international trade.

If they’re wrong, the roller coaster ride will still have some more fun in store for us. But as long as we eventually end our current experiment in “emergency” tariff dictatorship and get back to functioning as a democracy, things should be just fine in the long run. I’m still 100% invested myself, so that’s where I place my bet.

The Biggest Lesson: Don’t Form Your Opinions Based on News Headlines

Decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us, with just a bit of sizzle and spice to pull in our attention. Unfortunately, nowadays the priorities have flipped where the primary goal is attention, and accuracy carries little or no weight. Even a totally inaccurate article makes money for the publisher.

So while Democrats and Republicans like to do battle over which media sources are biased, in reality they’re all wrong: all click-funded commercial media is biased – sometimes politically but even more importantly biased towards generating outrage and fear, because those generate more money.

1) Either ignore the media completely and focus on your own life, or

2) Become a subject matter expert on things you really care about, and then read the original sources whenever you want to learn about something.

I mostly practice option #1, but as a science and technology nerd I get into #2 in just the areas I find most interesting. And it’s amazing how the more deeply you understand a subject, the more you see just how wrong most media stories are about your area of expertise. Which means they’re probably pretty wrong about almost everything.

So as always, with this lesson learned it’s time to shut down that phone and laptop, exhale all our worries and get back outside with your real-life family and friends. See you in a few months!

Great question – I tried to cover this in the article under the heading, “Why haven’t I noticed prices going up yet?”

First of all, most of the tariffs (or threatened tariffs) haven’t even hit yet.

But even when they do, the end result will be a bit unpredictable. Importers can of course shift supply to countries with lower tariffs or even domestic suppliers. Consumers will also react to rising prices by scaling back their spending, which shifts prices back down the supply/demand curve a little.

In the extreme case, high tariffs can even cause a recession which lowers demand for almost all goods and services, which means that prices for domestically produced services with elastic pricing might go down and bring the overall inflation numbers back in check. In other words, some people lose their jobs so on average there’s less money being spent on restaurants -> restaurants have to lower their prices.

Heck, in a good enough recession even house prices and rents will drop, which is the biggest factor in the inflation basket.

Might be semantic, but maybe tariffs are not “inflation”. It would be like saying that a VAT would be inflationary. At least food for thought – he posits that economists don’t actually think tariffs are inflationary.

100% the case. Inflation is caused by an increase in the money supply, by definition. It means your purchasing power is worth less. A one-time increase in a specific category of goods of 15% is not “inflation.” Meanwhile, every time the government uses printed (or digitally entered) dollars to spend trillions they don’t have, inflation grows massively and compounds, and for some reason, the majority of people don’t bat an eye.

A great analogy for inflation would be something like this… You are in charge of the county fair. There are a bunch of vendors of popcorn, cotton candy, and ride like ferris wheels, etc. You print tickets that visitors can use to acquire these goods and ride these rides, and the vendors set their own ticket prices. You and your friends discover you can give yourselves tickets and get more popcorn and ride more rides since you own the ticket machine. With the flood of tickets, the vendors realize they can (and need to) raise their prices. This is inflation. And it doesn’t matter if it’s due to your and your friends doing it for yourselves, or just doing it because of more guests coming to the fair (for “growth”).

I think the definition of inflation is a rise in prices not a rise in money supply. Money supply is one factor in that, but so is the overall supply and demand of everything that is for sale. Money supply is increased or decreased as needed in reaction to what’s happening with prices, in order to keep prices more stable, if the system is well managed.

In your county fair example, you are holding the number of vendors and the items and quantities for sale as a constant while increasing the number of tickets. In reality the fair’s mini-economy will grow and shrink over time, and if the ticket supply were forced to always stay constant the ticket prices of rides, popcorn and cotton candy would move up and down significantly in reaction.

“I think the definition of inflation is a rise in prices not a rise in money supply.”

Thank you for raising this point. The lack of concern about the impacts on businesses has been a real source of frustration for me.

My day job has given me a window into some industry sectors, including during Trump 1.0 and the trade war then. I always remember the small US steel manufacturer one of my colleagues spoke with at that time, when researching some of the impacts of steel tariffs.

The company was an important employer in its local area, producing steel canisters that it sold to a global slate of companies (so it was an exporter, and also sold domestically). Its main input was a particular type of steel pipe made in China (so it was also an importer). After Trump implemented steel tariffs, this small firm was suddenly paying an additional $250 million (back in 2018/2019; do your own inflation math as to what that would be today) at the US border before it could pick up a shipment.

It wasn’t going to be able to afford to stay open if it couldn’t get the administration to give it a tariff exemption (something Trump 1.0 was more willing to do, although the time involved to apply and, hopefully, get some sort of relief (many didn’t) meant companies were shelling out cash in the meantime). Why? Because not only did it not have a way to source the pipe in the US (steel is made to specification and you often can’t just readily swap things out), it couldn’t afford to do that because with a global client base, it needed to keep its pricing competitive (its customers could seek out non-US sources, unaffected by tariffs, for canisters instead).

We do actually have a manufacturing sector in the US. Most companies in that sector are small and midsized firms (fewer than 500 workers; often much smaller) and these may be important employers locally (although most employment in the industry overall is via the smaller number of very large firms); many are family firms. All sizes of manufacturer may import a raw material, a component or a finished good (including capital equipment for their facilities). When we tariff, we end up hurting our own manufacturing sector along the way. I lost track of the steel canister-maker’s fate, but I’ve never forgotten its difficulty, as just one illustration of tariff impacts that aren’t about the CPI.

But there’s also no real controversy (among people who study this stuff) in saying that tariffs tend to raise prices somewhere along the way, although it can take several months and may not be a straight $1 for $1 increase for end-consumers (although it often, eventually, is). I agree that it doesn’t create a prolonged rise in inflation (which is a rate of increase), but it does tend to eventually raise prices over a certain period and they then stay at that higher level. That’s actually part of how tariffs work, by putting a new floor under prices, reducing price competition.

And there are spillovers well beyond the firms initially impacted. For instance, US makers of tin plate, used in can-making, were hit by Trump 1.0’s steel tariffs, which jacked up their input costs (whether they continued with imports or switched to domestic sources — especially since domestic steel makers raised their own prices after tariffs were imposed on imports, an approach they’ve continued with in the latest trade war). This then made foreign-produced end-products such as canned food more attractive, because the pricing was better due to the lower production costs for non-US producers of tin plate. In other words, not only did US tin plate manufacturers suffer, but so did their US customers, as those companies’ customers looked elsewhere. (Trump’s much-broader trade war this time could offset some of this, by making imported canned goods more expensive, as well, depending on how things play out, which, in turn, would affect things like grocery store margins, etc.)

I also want to add that one of the biggest problems worrying the manufacturing industry for years, including pre-pandemic, has been the difficulty firms often face in filling the jobs they already have, and the difficulty they expect to face in filling jobs they expect to have due to a looming wave of retirements. This is due to several reasons: a skills gap (applicants not having the desired skill-sets); geographic miss-matches (jobs in one place, potential workers in another); problems with drug use in some communities (applicants are often expected to pass drug tests in order to operate machinery; the opioid epidemic has truly clobbered some communities in manufacturing areas); lack of interest among younger people in going into manufacturing or other production sectors (definitely something we need to work on; lack of exposure and training in K-12 is part of the trouble there, although the appeal of other types of work has also pulled potential workers elsewhere — maybe AI taking white collar jobs will sort that out?); and an increasing tightness in the overall US labor market due to demographics (ie, retirements on the aggregate, although jobs involving manual labor often see retirements at earlier ages, skewing the problem for those industries).

To finally conclude this overlong comment — which still barely scratches the surface; I didn’t even go into the tariff (and trade war) impacts on US shipping and logistics sectors tied to global trade, including imports — a major and rarely-discussed downside of tariffs is simply that it’s so difficult to readily see the ways they thread through an economy and create a drag on firms’ employment, wages/benefits, expansion plans, financing options, earnings and stock prices, and, yes, on consumer spending. The hits to businesses are often below the radar — especially since many companies don’t want to attract the anger of protectionists (unions; certain parts of the progressive wing; the Trump administration) by openly admitting how tariffs hurt their business. So people who aren’t trade geeks are understandably oblivious to real effects of these types of policies. As Cullen Roche over at Discipline Funds has repeatedly put it, with tariffs, you have less economic growth than you would have had — you just don’t know it.

The Biden administration and Dems in Congress (and sometimes even GOPers in Congress at that time, in some rare moments of bipartisanship) did several good things to directly support certain manufacturing and other production sectors (in my world I knew about policy for clean energy-related manufacturing; the defense industry; critical minerals; computer chips). Trump and the GOP have reduced or eliminated a chunk of that, unfortunately. But the recent tax bill did include some useful items for manufacturing. The GOP could do even more to directly support the sector, if manufacturing jobs are the real goal of all this, without the downsides of tariffs. (To be clear, this is not a political argument that I’m making; I didn’t like the tariffs imposed during the Biden admin, any more than Trump’s.)

2000 US Debt ($5.7 trillion) Source: https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/datasets/historical-debt-outstanding/historical-debt-outstanding

Current US Debt ($36.2 trillion Source: https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/datasets/historical-debt-outstanding/historical-debt-outstanding

2016 Nominal US GDP Growth (3.2%) Source: https://www.jec.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/34c0c783-f785-459c-a93a-2997c6abb8b4/01-30-gdp-review.pdf

2019 Nominal US GDP Growth (4.1%) Source: https://www.bea.gov/news/2020/gross-domestic-product-fourth-quarter-and-year-2019-advance-estimate#:~:text=Current%2Ddollar%20GDP%20increased%204.1,table%201%20and%20table%203).

US Federal deficit as percentage of GDP Source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FYFSGDA188S

Also, I think it’s worth flagging the US debt as a proportion of GDP, which is the key statistic vs. just thinking of the absolute figure. There are different ways to slice the US debt, but they all tell the same story. Just taking the basic total US debt relative to GDP shows a rise from 54% at year ending 2000 to 121% as of 1Q2025. That is staggeringly scary. Source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GFDEGDQ188S

Another after thought, while nominal GDP matters for the annual deficit, that is not to say real GDP doesn’t matter in a silo. They both have relevance. Clearly the US government has more control over expenses, and to a somewhat lesser extent revenue, than it does inflation. For 2024, the deficit ran at 6.28% of GDP. If inflation, which most of us can agree above a low percentage is typically bad, drops back into a ~2% range but real GDP growth runs in the 2-3% range, which is decent growth, then we’re still only growing nominal GDP at 4-5% vs. 6%+ under the state-of-play. Source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FYFSGDA188S) Source: https://www.bea.gov/news/2025/gross-domestic-product-4th-quarter-and-year-2024-second-estimate

This is an interesting analysis. The way I summed it up to an acquaintance is that Trump is playing with fire. In the end, it may be that we have something nice and shiny as a result. However, it is just as likely (if not more) that this whole thing is a dumpster fire and in the end it will just a smoking heap of ash.

However, the more fundamental problem here is that the reason that things like this (i.e., Trump unilaterally going tariff-nuclear, which is actually quite similar to what Biden did trying to illegally wipe out student loan debt, it’s just that Trump’s actions are at a different order of magnitude) is because Congress actively refuses to do their jobs. In the last several decades they have rather been rather determined to pass really loose/broad laws and specifically leave the “details” to the executive branch (either as some nebulous presidential power, or via some rule-making provision for an executive agency). This was bad but not terrible as long as we were electing presidents who were within a standard deviation of the ‘center’ of the political spectrum. However, Trump is a major outlier, and now it is readily apparent that Congress’ approach of letting the executive branch decide most things for itself isn’t actually a really good idea.

Even going back to the difference between Trump’s use of tariffs and Biden’s student debt cancellation efforts, it is clear that Biden’s policy, while objectively of very dubious legality, didn’t move the macroeconomic needle. Trump’s policies, on the other hand, even if they turn out to be completely legal (which I’m not sure they will), are rather painful object lesson on why Congress needs to actually do their jobs with a bit more effort.

A stray bit of additional perspective: A good friend of mine lost a large swath of her extended family when covid churned through northern Italy in the first year of the pandemic. Communities in their area suffered terrible losses that upended the social fabric overall, in addition to the grief suffered by specific families.

This also happened in many parts of the US, with certain kinds of communities hit particularly hard (groups that tend to live with extended family were especially vulnerable; non-hispanic white middle- and upper-class America is least-likely to live that way, so people from that type of background may not have seen much of this directly).

Given what NYC itself went through early in that first year, it also wouldn’t surprise me if NYT staffers genuinely felt horrified at what was happening. My friends and colleagues living in NYC certainly felt that way, based on what they were seeing and experiencing directly themselves.

So yes, it’s absolutely true that all forms of heart disease combined remained the number one cause of death in both 2020 and 2021, followed by all cancers combined. But I suspect that many people whose families and communities were gutted by covid would agree with the NYT that the toll from that new cause of death was terrible, and that it was something worth being concerned about, even if covid alone ended up being the third-leading cause of US deaths in both of those years, after which broad herd immunity finally set in.

Also, if anyone has an idea for how to fund newspaper journalism such that eyeballs aren’t the thing, I know several very good journalists who would *love* to hear what it is. (Pricier subscriptions can’t be the answer; not if you want to pay decent salaries and thus keep people around so that you have a good mix of entry-level people and experienced folks, and not if you want to include small and regional news outlets in your funding model — you could never charge enough for subscriptions for a local or even regional paper for that to cover all costs and still have a decent staff, both in terms of actual size and experience mix. This applies to both digital and hard-copy papers.)

If you do not think that the NYT serves a political agenda, the you are naïve.

And while I think that Pete’s nostalgic comment (“Decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us…”) is equally naïve, he recognizes that today news organizations are driven by getting eyeballs on their content. The thing is, it’s always been like this. Certainly, the intensity has varied with times and places, but yellow journalism (the type of sensationalism that characterizes nearly 100% of mass media coverage today) originated in the 1880s in NYC. Back then the NYT didn’t lower themselves to that level, but it’s pretty obvious that today they are down there and they deserve to be compared to the likes of FoxNews, MSNBC, and so forth.

I think a useful comparison that illustrates something important about the NYT is to look at its news articles and compare them with those in the Wall Street Journal (owned by News Corp, by the way, as is Fox News). Both the NYT and WSJ are dealing with a crazy-ass environment for “newspapers” vs back in the day. And both approach their news journalism in a similar way, even if the specific type of news story they do may differ.

At the same time, nothing could be more different than their respective opinion sections — both the editorials by their editorial boards and those by columnists and guests are 180-degrees opposite from each other much of the time.

In other words, in terms of political-ish stance, they are radically different. In terms of journalism? Pretty similar: fact-based, attempting to give a full picture, and corrections if someone messes something up. They entertain if they can, but it’s secondary to information provision.

I can’t say the same about Fox News (which I used to watch some years ago, but stopped when I realized I was never really going to get a full picture of anything since it wasn’t their style). They are really an entertainment-first entity, and they are facing fierce competition from Newsmax, which has made it less and less appealing for them to say anything they think their viewers might not want to hear. (That said, I’ve found the online version of their sister product, Fox Business, to be helpful at times. Just as I like CNBC’s “state of freight” pages for some aspects of tariff impacts on shipping and warehousing. Written! Not the videos/cable shows for either of these. There’s usually more information in written material, and the potential for more nuance. (Not always fulfilled, alas).)

With all due respect, you, and unfortunately, many others, are missing the point.

We (and Trump) get that the cost will get passed onto the consumers. Or at least that’s the “first order effect” (to borrow your phrase.)

What you’re missing is that consumers get to decide between whether to purchase the item or not. If they are willing to eat the cost, and the item is something they absolutely can’t live without, they’ll buy it. Or they won’t buy it at all.

In the latter case, the sales numbers (and thus revenue) of the company selling the goods will drop. At which point that company has a choice to make: live with the drop in sales, and thus bottom line, eat part of the tariff or all of it, in order to increase volume.

Obviously, the company’s goal (let’s use Nike as an example), is to make as much money as possible. So if they naively pass 100% of the cost onto the consumer, their sales might drop so much that they’ll realize that wasn’t the best financial decision. This is an optimization problem: find the global maximum. The variables are: what % of tariffs to eat (vs pass on), whether to continue to offshore or onshore (and to what degree), and so on.

Using the Nike example (because they recently sobbed about their $1Bn tariff bill), their product is, among other things, athletic shoes. They’re not an essential item. They’re a luxury. It’s also not something you buy every week. Consumers can easily forego purchasing a new pair of Nike shoes, and Nike can decide if it can stomach the sales drop or not and react accordingly. That’s not our concern. We shouldn’t feel sorry for Nike who got rich at the expense of exploiting sweat job labor and pocketing the enormous margins, while selling out American jobs.

The other second-order effect you missed is the fact that by creating these “tariff walls” the money stays onshore. I.e. customers buy US-made goods and pay local companies, i.e. their fellow citizen. The money feeds back into the US economy. Without them, even though goods are “cheaper” for the consumer, the money flows out of the country: enriching China and other third world countries at our expense. What are some third-order effects you think might arise from that? I hope you see how this thinking is a bit short-sighted.

#8378. Adventurer to Climb 100 Peaks on 2,000Km Taiwan Traverse

Tomorrow, November 1, Japanese adventurer Yoki Tanaka begins a four-month, 2,000km trek north to south down the length of Taiwan. Along the way, he will summit all 100 of Taiwan’s celebrated Baiyue peaks.

Taiwan has about 268 peaks exceeding 3,000m, but only 100 of them made this special list, which is based not only on height but beauty, difficulty, prominence, and character. Prominent Taiwanese mountaineers compiled the list in the early 1970s, partly inspired by Japan’s own list of 100 revered mountains.

Yoki Tanaka arrives in Taiwan earlier this week. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

The 43-year-old Tanaka has specialized in this unusual combination of long-distance trekking and mountaineering. In 2014, he summited Japan’s 100 famous mountains while walking 7,800km over 208 days. (Japan, though far bigger than Taiwan, has only 23 mountains over 3,000m.) A year later, he extended that by climbing 200 mountains and walking 8,000km in 222 days. Finally, he increased that again to 300 mountains. This time, it took him three years and about 20,000km of walking.

Tanaka will begin on Sunday from the northernmost tip of Taiwan, at the Cape Fugui lighthouse, and finish sometime in March at Eluanbi, the country’s southernmost point. The first 150km will be along roads before he reaches his first trailhead. He’ll spend the next week trekking. His first five peaks will be Xueshan (3,886m), Nanhudashan (3,742m), Hehuanshan (3,417m), Qilaishan (3,560m), and Nenggaoshan 3,262m).

Although he won’t use motorized transport for the entire journey, he will have ample opportunity to resupply along the way. His expedition plan includes a charmingly precise breakdown of how he plans to spend his evenings: town stays, 48 days; mountain huts, 38 days; tent camping, 39 days. He has also budgeted 16 rest days and 20 contingency days.

Tanaka trains in Taiwan earlier this year. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

His most difficult section, scheduled for early January, will take him through the remote interior of the Central Mountain Range for over two weeks. During this time, he’ll have to carry his own food, search for trails that may no longer exist, and gamble that he will be able to find enough water.

During a December 2025 reconnaissance trip to Xueshan, Taiwan’s second-highest mountain, Tanaka discovered how difficult it can be to obtain water. Two water sources marked on his map were completely dry.

On a previous hike. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

By late January, the Japanese trekker should reach the historic Batongguan Trail, eventually leading to 3,952m Yushan, Taiwan’s highest mountain. The Batongguan Trail was originally constructed in 1875 under the Qing dynasty to establish a route across the mountainous interior. Decades later, Japanese colonial authorities constructed a separate crossing through the region. Sections of the route survive as remote hiking trails and provide access to some of Taiwan’s highest mountains.

Tanaka first visited Taiwan in the spring of 2025 and has made several reconnaissance visits since, including an east-west crossing of the island earlier this year. He had intended to begin his Taiwan 100 Peaks Traverse project this past spring, but local mountaineers advised him to avoid the rainy season and typhoon risks. Their advice prompted him to shift his starting date to November.

Yoki Tanaka on a training hike in Taiwan. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

Interestingly, of Taiwan’s 100 Baiyue peaks, only 99 are now recognized as surpassing 3,000m. The exception is Lushan at 2,981m. It was originally measured at 3,043m but subsequent measurements reduced its elevation. Nevertheless, it remains on the list.

Taiwan’s representative in Japan told Japanese media that the fastest prior completion of the Baiyue by a foreign climber took three years and eight months, spread over multiple trips.

Once Tanaka begins, his expedition website will provide live tracking of his progress across Taiwan.

Jerry Kobalenko is the editor of ExplorersWeb. One of Canada’s premier arctic travelers, he is the author of The Horizontal Everest and Arctic Eden, and has just finished a book about adventures in Labrador. In 2018, he was awarded the Polar Medal by the Governor General of Canada and in 2022, he received the Queen’s Platinum Jubilee Medal for services to exploration.

ExplorersWeb is part of AllGear Digital's portfolio of media brands.

Hire one nanny together with another family, and each family usually pays about two-thirds of a nanny’s going rate while the nanny earns a third more. Put the nanny share’s terms in writing first, including how much notice a family gives before leaving, and pay the payroll taxes on your own share.

Care.com’s 2026 Cost of Care Report puts the average cost of a nanny for one child at $870 for a 40-hour week, or $21.75 an hour. At two-thirds of that, each family in a share pays about $580 a week instead of $870, roughly $15,000 less over a year.

The nanny comes out ahead too. Two families paying $14.50 an hour each give the nanny $29 an hour, a third more than the $21.75 one family pays, for watching both families’ children at once.

At about $580 a week, a share still costs more than a day care center, which averages $332 a week in the same report. The extra $248 a week buys care in a home with one other family’s children instead of a center’s classroom.

Look for a family nearby that needs care during the same hours and has a child close in age to yours. Then ask what nannies near you charge one family, and set each family’s share at about two-thirds of that rate.

Each family pays the nanny its share separately and counts as a household employer, so each owes Social Security and Medicare taxes once its pay for the year reaches the IRS threshold.

Put the terms in writing before the first day, starting from the nanny share work agreement that Hand in Hand, a nonprofit network of household employers, publishes. Settle at least these:

A family that quits the share leaves the other paying for a nanny of its own, $21.75 an hour at the national average instead of $14.50, until a new family joins. Agree up front that a family leaving gives at least four weeks’ notice or keeps paying its share for four weeks.

#8373. Everest 1971: Ambition, Death, and Dispute

In the spring of 1971, only one party attempted to climb Everest. Led by Norman Dyhrenfurth and Jimmy Roberts, this ambitious expedition planned to split into two groups. One party would go for the steep Southwest Face, while the other would attempt the West Ridge.

It was meant to be as much a test of international cooperation as an extraordinary climbing effort. But what happened turned out to be more complicated and controversial than anyone had expected.

Before the team even arrived in Nepal, the venture was heavily commercialized and advertised to the public. The BBC secured exclusive television rights and embedded a nine-person film crew directly into the expedition. At the same time, the British newspaper rights were sold to The Sunday Times, which sent along prominent journalists like Murray Sayle. The media machinery relentlessly hyped the expedition beforehand, boldly framing the climb as a mere formality and setting public expectations for a historic success.

The expedition itself came from a merger of two plans. A British-Norwegian group asked Roberts to lead a Southwest Face attempt. Dyhrenfurth was already organizing the same route, so they joined forces. As the combined team was large, they decided to try two routes at once.

The Southwest Face was the main goal, specifically aiming for a direct, vertical line (a direttissima), while the other group targeted the complete, aesthetic West Ridge route. Both goals were very difficult, and climbers chose their preferred route.

Jimmy Roberts in Nepal. Photo: The Nepal Times

The Southwest Face team included British climbers Dougal Haston and Don Whillans, Japanese climbers Naomi Uemura and Reizo Ito, and others. The West Ridge team included Austrian Wolfgang Axt, Swiss climbers Michel and Yvette Vaucher, Norwegian climbers Odd Eliassen and Jon Teigland, American David Isles, and Indian Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna. Frenchman Pierre Mazeaud and Italian Carlo Mauri later joined the West Ridge side.

In total, the whole expedition had 31 foreign climbers from a dozen countries, as well as several Sherpas, including Ang Phurba and Sonam Girme. According to early planning notes, neither leader had personal summit ambitions. Both described themselves as the older men of the team.

The Southwest Face of Everest. Photo: Wikimedia

Base Camp was established on March 22, 1971, at 5,425m. Both teams worked through the Khumbu Icefall. Dyhrenfurth later said it was in the most difficult and dangerous state he had ever seen it. They set up Advance Base Camp on the Western Cwm, then separated.

The Southwest Face team pushed higher. The West Ridge team, with Axt as coordinator, began setting up their own camps, although supplies arrived slowly. Some of the West Ridge climbers didn’t want to carry heavy loads. A long storm in late April made conditions worse for both teams and delayed everything by two to three weeks. Dyhrenfurth’s own account in the American Alpine Journal confirms the early harmony among the team and the exceptional difficulties of the Icefall that spring.

The 1971 Everest expedition. Photo: ‘Surrender to Everest’/imdb.com

On April 18, Bahuguna and Axt of the West Ridge team were descending from a high camp in a storm at about 7,000m. They were not tied to each other. Axt had left his harness and climbing rope higher up to save weight, knowing fixed ropes were already in place. He crossed a long fixed-rope traverse by hand, waited for Bahuguna, saw him wave, then continued down because he was exhausted. He later heard screams and raised the alarm.

A rescue party reached Bahuguna still clipped to the fixed rope, about 25m from easier ground. He had lost a mitten and a crampon, and his face was covered by ice. Attempts to lower him failed in the storm and darkness, and he finally died of cold and exhaustion. Bahuguna’s fingers and face were crusted with ice, his eyes were wide, and he could not recognize Whillans or speak.

Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna on the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal

According to Roberts’ report in the Himalayan Database, the rescuers had to leave Bahuguna because it would be completely dark in 10 minutes, and the others would freeze too. Roberts later described the death as the result of a series of mistakes by Bahuguna and Axt themselves, and noted that allowing them to go so high alone had been a factor.

Bahuguna’s body was later recovered and cremated near Base Camp.

Dyhrenfurth held an inquiry after the fatal incident. Axt said that the fixed ropes made roping up unnecessary and that he didn’t realize how serious things were until the screams. He later explained that if he had stayed longer, he risked losing his own fingers and toes.

“What should I do? One hour later and I am frozen,” he said. He added that he couldn’t pull Bahuguna himself and had to go down for fresh men.

Mazeaud called it murder through negligence. Dyhrenfurth agreed that Axt should have gone back to look, but said that it was easy to judge after the event. Roberts noted that Bahuguna’s death was very sad but didn’t determine the expedition’s final outcome.

Norman Dyhrenfurth, Carlo Mauri, Yvette Vaucher, Reizo Ito, Pierre Mazeaud, and Michale Vaucher in ‘Surrender to Everest’ (1971). Photo: imdb.com

After the death and the storm, most of the remaining West Ridge climbers (especially Mazeaud, Mauri and the Vauchers) wanted to abandon both hard routes and switch to the normal South Col route. They said that it was more practical and gave a better chance of reaching the summit.

Many others, including most of the Southwest Face group and the leading Sherpas, believed that those climbers mainly wanted personal success: first Frenchman, first Italian, or first woman. A vote that included the Sherpas went strongly in favor of putting all remaining effort into the Southwest Face. The West Ridge group said the decision was a plot to keep them off the summit, so the press would stay focused on the Southwest Face.

Camp 2. Pumori on the left, with snow-and-ice slopes leading to the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal

Mazeaud’s radio message said that they expected him — a French member of parliament — to work like a Sherpa for Anglo-Saxons and Japanese. He said France had been insulted. Yvette Vaucher called the decision monstrous and said she had lost Everest and her friends at the same time.

According to one account, Roberts told Mazeaud to leave during a loud argument. The four went home in early May, ending further work on the West Ridge. Isles and Teigland later said that the decision to cancel the West Ridge climb, made in a highly emotional moment after Bahuguna’s death, was a great mistake. Teigland said he had dreamed of the West Ridge for two years.

A virus, diagnosed by some as mononucleosis, spread through the camps and forced many climbers down, including Dyhrenfurth. Bad weather continued to block supplies. With the West Ridge group gone and fewer people left, Haston and Whillans kept pushing on the Southwest Face. Japanese climbers and Sherpas carried heavy loads high on the mountain. Camps were placed up to approx. 8,290m.

Haston and Whillans fixed ropes partway into a chimney in the Rock Band but ran out of rope, oxygen, and food. According to Roberts, they placed Camp 6 at 8,290m and were making progress every day. He said they could have traversed onto the South Buttress and reached the summit that way in one day, but that was not the route they had come to climb. Extreme cold hampered them. They needed another camp higher up. They turned back 450m short of the summit on May 21.

Roberts later said weather was the basic cause of failure: Once it goes bad, it affects everything else. He described the expedition as 50 percent successful. They failed to summit, but those who stayed worked well together.

Roberts said that he was bitterly disappointed after three years of work, but apart from Bahuguna’s death, he had nothing to regret. He criticized Schloemmer for contributing almost nothing and said that Axt was asked to come up and help on the Southwest Face but thought it over and went down instead.

Haston called claims that the Austrians were ready to help “complete balls.” He said that when they asked for support at Camp 5, Schloemmer replied that he needed a Sherpa to carry his personal gear. Haston added that he and Whillans were the only ones who could push hard enough to get the route going, and that the Japanese were the only others with real high-Himalayan experience.

Uemura said that he and Ito helped by carrying loads because that was their obligation, and that if the weather had been good, the expedition could have succeeded. After the 1971 expedition, Uemura decided to always climb solo thereafter.

Axt and Schloemmer complained there was no real authority above Advance Base Camp. Axt said the two British stayed high for three weeks and monopolized the lead, and that without a coordinator to rotate people, there was no room for others. He said if there had been good organization on the Face, he could have succeeded. Isles and Teigland said the international aspect had nothing to do with the failure.

The problems came from personalities and the emotional decision after the death. Mazeaud and the Vauchers maintained that the leaders had broken the original plan of two routes and prevented them from reaching the summit for publicity reasons. Dyhrenfurth said the experiment in international climbing was only partially successful, but cooperation had been good until the argument over the route. He noted that the United Nations had tried international cooperation for a long time and had not done too well, either.

In their interesting and detailed post-climb article titled Post-Mortem of an International Expedition for Mountain magazine (later reprinted by The Himalayan Club), authors Ken Wilson and Mike Pearson traced exactly how the initial merger and massive team size doomed the expedition from the start. They concluded that the 1971 expedition’s collapse was primarily driven by severe natural forces, specifically adverse weather and illness, rather than interpersonal friction. They also attributed systemic blame to organizers for combining distinct climbing factions into an unmanageable, oversized team.

Memorial at Everest in 1971 for Harsh Bahuguna. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal

The questions remain: Was Bahuguna’s death mainly the result of mistakes by the two men involved, or something the leaders should have prevented? Did the decision to drop the West Ridge and focus on the Southwest Face save the expedition or destroy it? And was the international idea itself the problem, or simply the mix of strong personalities, bad weather, and the pressure of being on Everest?

KrisAnnapurna is a writer with ExplorersWeb.

Kris has been writing about history and tales in alpinism, news, mountaineering, and news updates in the Himalaya, Karakoram, etc., for with ExplorersWeb since 2021. Prior to that, Kris worked as a real estate agent, interpreter, and translator in criminal law. Now based in Madrid, Spain, she was born and raised in Hungary.

#8364. Karl Bushby Reaches Mother's House, Ending 28-Year Journey Around the World

“This is absolute madness,” said a happy Karl Bushby, as hundreds of people welcomed him home in a civic ceremony in his hometown of Hull, England. In a scene that couldn’t be more different from the past 28 years that he has spent walking around the world, Bushby stood underneath a giant Welcome Home Karl sign, made an appreciative speech, then begged off to continue walking the final few steps to his mother’s house, which he left back in 1998.

The reunion with his mother a couple of hours later was equally public, as the pair were surrounded by TV cameras and hundreds of well-wishers.

When Karl Bushby quietly set off from the southern tip of South America on November 1 of that year, it was very different. Bushby was 29 years old. He is now 57. When he began, he had around $500 in his pocket, a two-wheeled cart loaded with supplies, and an idea that most people would have dismissed as a fantasy. He was going to walk home to Hull, England, without using any transport. He would not return to the UK until he could do so on foot. He expected the expedition to take about 12 years. Instead, it has taken 28.

Bushby has spent more than 10,000 days and 50,000km pursuing that single objective. The Goliath Expedition has become one of the longest and most unusual human-powered adventures in modern exploration, and he is nervous about it ending. Speaking to The Washington Post as he approached home, he said: “My purpose and reason for living is about to end. It’s going to be difficult…trying to blend back into a society that you just don’t know anymore.”

Through Chile’s Atacama Desert. Photo: Karl Bushby

While serving with the Parachute Regiment, Bushby received a birthday card from his father, Keith, who had served in the British Army. In it was a story about special forces soldiers debating whether it was possible to walk from London to New York via the Bering Strait. Looking at a world map, Bushby began tracing the route himself.

But rather than stopping at New York, he extended the line south through the Americas, all the way to the tip of Chile. The result was an expedition that would take him from the southernmost reaches of South America back to his home in England.

“That was the moment the hairs on the back of your neck stand up,” he told GQ Magazine. “You think, well, that’s it.” He did some calculations, created a timeline on the “back of a beer mat,” and estimated the journey would take him 12 years. From that point, Bushby showed nothing but determination. At the start, most people doubted it was even possible. That only made him more certain that he wanted to try.

He gave himself two rules. The first was that he could not use any transportation, even self-propelled vehicles like bicycles or kayaks, to advance the expedition. The second was that he could not return to the UK until he had completed the walk. Those rules sound simple. In practice, they created multiple logistical nightmares and affected almost every aspect of his life.

Bushby left Punta Arenas, Chile, with his equipment loaded onto a cart he calls The Beast. He was not an elite endurance athlete embarking on a carefully funded and organized expedition. He was a young former paratrooper with a few hundred dollars, a rough line on a map, and limited resources. He had no supporters or funding, and relied on gas station food or what locals gave him.

“The first years, you’re living the boys’ adventure dream, and it’s great,” he told The New York Times, “and then it really becomes a grind.”

The first few years took him north through the Americas, including multiple conflict zones. In Peru, he was attacked by a mob; in Colombia, he floated down the crocodile-laden Atrato River to avoid being spotted by armed men. Then he faced the Darien Gap, that infamously dangerous stretch between Colombia and Panama, ruled by drug and human smugglers, that almost all adventurers skirt around.

Eventually, he reached Panama. But emerging from the jungle did not mean he was free to continue. After crossing a restricted border zone without the necessary visa, he was detained for 18 days.

After making his way through the Americas, Bushby eventually finished crossing the U.S., where he had picked up a few sponsorships, and reached Alaska. The next major obstacle, and the one that catapulted his journey into world news, was the Bering Strait, the stretch of water separating North America from Russia.

The Arctic had already given Bushby a taste of its dangers. During the Alaskan stage of the expedition, he was rescued by helicopter after becoming stranded on an ice floe that broke away from the coast and drifted out to sea, and had a standoff with a polar bear. He knew how risky the Bering Strait crossing would be.

In March 2006, Bushby and French adventurer Dimitri Kieffer spent 14 days crossing the Bering Strait between Alaska and Russia on foot. With 90kg sleds, they traveled across the shifting ice in temperatures that fell to around -30˚C, against the prevailing winds as the ice moved beneath them.

Wearing dry suits, they had to swim at points through the icy, slushy water. “All night long, you’re just listening to the grinding, and the ice is just like screaming,” he told The New York Times. “We actually had to evacuate the tent during the night because the thing started to break apart beneath us.”

They made it across, achieving a rare crossing of one of the world’s most formidable natural barriers. But reaching Russia did not mean the difficulties were over. Russian authorities detained the pair for entering the country without the required permission. They faced the possibility of deportation.

Crossing the Bering Strait. Photo: Karl Bushby

Russia would consume years of Bushby’s life. He had to leave the country every 90 days because his tourist visa allowed him to stay in Russia for only 90 of every 180 days. Then in 2008, his journey came to a standstill. He lost sponsorship and could not travel to Russia for a few years. In 2011, he resumed his trek, again in 90-day stints. Then in 2012, he was denied a further visa, and in 2013, he received a five-year entry ban from Russia.

Here, Bushby responded with an extraordinary protest. He walked approximately 5,000km from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., hoping to draw attention to his predicament and secure the paperwork he needed to continue.

The years of delay exposed another unusual aspect of the expedition. Bushby’s rules did not mean he had to remain indefinitely in the country where he was stuck. Nor did they prevent him from using transport for journeys unrelated to advancing his route home. However, he couldn’t fly back to the UK during these hiatuses.

When visas, funding, or political restrictions prevented him from continuing, he could fly elsewhere, take a break, and wait until circumstances allowed him to resume. But he could not use that flight to skip a section of the route. Whenever he returned, he had to pick up from the exact point where he had stopped. Most of the time, he decamped to Mexico. Its lower cost of living made it a practical place to wait. He also spent time in the United States.

Bushby and Dimitri Kieffer, 2006. Photo: Karl Bushby

The distinction mattered enormously to the expedition. Bushby could board a plane to escape a logistical dead end, but when he returned to the route, he had to pick up where he had stopped. He could not simply fly over the awkward section and resume walking on the other side.

The arrangement might seem to stretch the definition of walking around the world. But for Bushby, it was the only way to maintain his two original rules without spending years of his life waiting at a closed border. Some visa delays took years to resolve. And the longer the journey continued, the harder it became to predict when, or even whether, it would end. Getting across Russia alone took almost 10 years.

He lived cheaply but still needed money to survive on this near-endless journey. Some of it came from the sponsorships he eventually acquired. During what sounded like a particularly low point 15 years ago, on one of his hiatuses in Mexico while trying to overcome another logistical hurdle on his journey, he told Backpacker magazine:

I’m 42 years old and I’m broke and I’m homeless. I’m a professional parasite. I’m a professional hobo. I’m sleeping on other people’s couches. I’m 42 years old, and I have to walk other people’s dogs, just so they’ll feed me. My job is picking up dog shit!

The passage of time is one of the most striking aspects of Bushby’s story. His expedition began in an era before smartphones, Instagram, and the expectation of sharing every stage of an adventure online. The young man who left Chile in 1998 could never have imagined that nearly three decades later, people around the world would be following his progress toward his childhood home. The fact that so many people are following it still baffles Bushby.

While Bushby was away, life continued for the people he had left behind. His son, Adam, grew up, and his family had to get on with their lives without him. Adam was eight when he set off. He is now 36, with a family of his own, including a 12-year-old daughter whom Bushby has never met.

When his dad started the walk, Adam didn’t fully understand what was going on, or know how to explain it to people who asked. Over the years, they have tried to stay in touch and maintain some kind of relationship. At 14, Adam flew to Alaska to see his dad. It was six years after the expedition began and a turning point for him in accepting what Bushby was doing. “I did feel a bit awkward because at that point I didn’t really know my dad,” he told GQ Magazine.

They later spent 10 days walking together as part of a National Geographic documentary project. Adam described the experience as surreal, suddenly stepping into his father’s world. They have spoken regularly since, but as Adam put it: “[His] life went this way, and I went that way, two separate routes.”

In various interviews, Adam has explained that he had nothing against his father’s ambition, that he respects what he has done and is very proud of him. But also that growing up without him had been difficult.

Karl Bushby has not seen other members of his family for years. He met Adam when he stepped out of the water after crossing the English Channel back to England, but he has not seen his mother in over a decade, even though he will be living with her once he arrives back at his childhood home. He recognizes how difficult the situation will be and that it is due to his choices over the last 30 years.

“The relationship between me and my son is good, but there’s a lot to resolve there,” he told GQ Magazine. “I’ve got a granddaughter I’ve never seen, and then dear old mother, Lord. I have to live with my mother now. I’m going from a global adventure to living with my mother in a basement at 57. This is going to be a challenge.”

Life on the road has often been lonely, but Bushby has seen kindness and hospitality in every corner of the globe. “I’ve been welcomed in by the poorest of the poor,” he told The Washington Post. “I’ve met 99.9999% of the very best of humanity. Every culture, every country, has been the same response.”

He has also had two significant romantic relationships during the expedition. He spent around seven years with a Colombian woman. Later, he had a three-year relationship with a woman from Japan. He met both while on the expedition, and it was also the reason both broke down.

After finally getting across Russia, Bushby continued through Mongolia, where he joined with other adventurers, including Angela Maxwell, to trek across the Gobi Desert with camels. After 1,130km and several disagreements, the group went their separate ways, and Busby continued into China by himself. In 2018, he crossed Kazakhstan and then made his way through Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. Once again, visa issues ground the journey to a standstill. He could not get into Iran.

At the same time, the world was struck down by the pandemic. More years of waiting in Mexico began, even though Bushby still had a substantial distance to cover. Eventually, in 2022, he was on the move again. Once again joined by Angela Maxwell, he did something he had never intended doing during the expedition — swimming across the Caspian Sea.

Visa issues and geopolitics meant he was unable to cross into Iran. So he came up with a new plan. He and Maxwell went back to Uzbekistan and took a different route. They walked across the Kyzylkum Desert until they reached the Caspian Sea. A self-proclaimed terrible swimmer, he was completely outside of his comfort zone. Wearing a wetsuit and flotation equipment, he described his floating-and-swimming hybrid as floatimming. It might not have been the most elegant crossing, but after 32 days at sea, 27 of which he was swimming with Maxwell and two Azerbaijani swimmers in very choppy waters, he completed the 288km swim.

Back on solid ground, his next job was to get across Azerbaijan and into Turkey. Here, he hit a huge milestone. He crossed the Bosphorus Bridge on May 2, 2025. This meant he was back in Europe for the first time since he started walking.

The remaining distance to Britain was comparatively short, but the final stages were not straightforward. Once again, visa restrictions were the thorn in his side. Limited to traveling for 90 days at a time before having to leave Europe, he continued to use Mexico as a base as he waited for his 90 days to reset and tackled the remaining distance in short stretches.

He made it through Turkey, Bulgaria, and Romania before confronting the next issue. Bushby always knew one of the logistical challenges would be getting from France to England. He started trying to pull a plan together. Unsurprisingly, for someone who has walked across the world, his goal was to cross it via the Channel Tunnel. The issue was that this was forbidden. He had hoped to use their service tunnel, but his request was denied.

Karl Bushby speaks at a civic ceremony in Hull, England earlier today. Photo: YouTube

As he continued walking through Hungary and Austria, he attempted to appeal the decision, reaching out to anyone who might help, to no avail. “We have carefully considered his request and explored a range of possible options. In this instance, regretfully, we are unable to accommodate Mr Bushby’s wishes,” a spokesperson for the Eurotunnel told the BBC. This meant the only alternative was to get back into the water and swim the Channel.

Still walking, he had made it to Germany. Then he picked his way across Belgium and France, all the while decamping to Mexico, Canada, or the U.S. every 90 days, and trying to piece together a plan for swimming the Channel. This proved to be another headache regarding permissions.

French rules stop anyone swimming the Channel from France to Britain. He thought he had been granted an exemption, but in September, he learned that was not the case. After much negotiation, he finally got the go-ahead. On October 5, Bushby finally landed back on British soil at Shakespeare Beach near Dover after swimming the English Channel.

The crossing took three days. He spent around 20 hours in the water, spent the nights on a safety vessel, and dropped back into the water at his last-known position each morning.

After 28 years abroad, he was finally back in the country he had left in 1998. But rather than feeling joy, he told The New York Times he felt a real sense of loss. After three decades on the road, the prospect of just 400km to go was hugely daunting. “I’m about to lose my purpose for living,” he said. “It’s about to abruptly end.”

He is nervous about what comes next and reintegrating into a society he no longer knows. He is considering retraining as a teacher, as he loved giving talks in schools as he walked.

One big question is why Bushby has become so celebrated. He is not the first person to have attempted a long-distance walk around the world. Other adventurers have spent years traveling between countries, crossing continents on foot, or undertaking journeys without motorized transport, but Bushby has singularly captured the world’s attention.

Karl Bushby, back turned, leaves the civic ceremony to walk the last few steps to his mother’s house. Photo: YouTube

It might be the particular combination of his rules, or the fact that his objective is immediately understandable. He left home, and he is walking back. There is no complicated scientific mission to explain, no specialized equipment that the public needs to understand, and no obscure record category he is aiming for. The simplicity of it gives the story an almost fable-like quality, even though the journey was not simple at all.

With just two rules, the expedition is relatively easy to follow. Every delay matters because Bushby cannot simply skip ahead. He is forced to wait or find another solution when something blocks his route. The question becomes how he will get around it without abandoning his principles.

Then there is the sheer amount of time it has taken. People who first encountered Bushby’s expedition in their twenties are now well into middle age themselves. Initially, there were no updates on social media. Instead, there was the odd news article that cropped up every few years about the same man, still walking across the world. A story that seemed like an ambitious adventure morphed into an entire adult life on the road.

Bushby has not necessarily made the journey look enjoyable. His progress has depended as much, if not more, on navigating bureaucracy and finding support as on putting one foot in front of the other. Despite it all, he continued.

As the journey has hit an era where we can follow an adventurer’s progress in real time, every obstacle and milestone has renewed interest in the question that has followed Bushby for 28 years: Will he actually make it home?

Now that he has to confront a new question: How do you cope with coming home after three decades? “I will have to figure out who I am again. What is the meaning to it all? How do I find that meaning and purpose? How do I fill that hole I’m suddenly going to find myself in?” he told the BBC in the days before the expected end of the expedition. “I think the old adage goes…the only thing worse than a man who can’t fulfill his dreams is a man who’s fulfilled his dreams…because then what?”

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

ExplorersWeb is part of AllGear Digital's portfolio of media brands.
